newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia seen linking car imports to exports.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia seen linking car imports to exports.

text.p: Yugoslavian producers of car components and semi-finished products called on Wednesday for a change in foreign trade regulations and asked that car imports be linked to the sale of their products abroad.
Producers said they would support a government decision to allow imports of 12,000 cars in 1997 but insisted on a matching level of exports and proposed a one to one ratio.

"We must take care of domestic industries when importing. Car imports must be conditional on the sale of domestic car components and semi-finished products abroad," said Ljubivoje Todorovic, the Yugoslav chamber of commerce official.

"The chamber supports imports from foreign firms that have invested their capital upgrading technology and improving production here. Tariffs on car imports should be reduced if the imports are linked to exports," he told Reuters.

Crippled by the violent break-up of Yugoslavia, mismanagement and almost four years of war-related sanctions, industries are struggling to return to the world market to provide urgently needed capital to kick-start production.

"Our factories can still produce high quality engine oil and air filters, shock absorbers, batteries and other car components for renowned world producers, as they used to do before the sanctions," said Todorovic, who heads the chamber's industry board.
"By linking car imports to exports we just want to re-activate production and increase capacity utilisation in our factories."

Car imports in 1996 were worth $42 million. Importers say there is a great need for high quality cars in a market where the average age of about 1.2 million cars in the country is 10 years and some 40 percent are older than 12 years.
It is rare to see anything other than locally-made Zastava cars throughout Serbia.

"With an average monthly wage of about 200 German marks and an insolvent banking sector there cannot be any satisfactory car sales," said Velimir Pijevic, general manager of Renault Kep, Renault's Yugoslavian dealer.
Car importers expressed doubts the entire import quota of 12,000 cars set for this year would be sold.
Renault Kep sold 200 cars in 1996 and planned to double its sales this year. "But considering the present economic environment we would be happy if sales remained at the 1996 level," he said.
Importers argue that even if taxes were cut, which now raise prices by up to 80 percent, sales would not improve.
"People simply do not have the money," Pijevic said.
Conditioning car imports with exports could make sales even more difficult as local producers cannot offer good quality products at adequate prices, importers say.

"Foreign partners want the best quality at the lowest price and many domestic producers cannot meet those standards and therefore are not competitive abroad," Rajko Djordjevic of Autocommerce said. "Producers here are as poor as the buyers." -- Belgrade Newsroom 381 11 222 4254
